newsitem.title: UK: Romania's king pleads for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Romania's king pleads for NATO membership.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael said on Wednesday that his country had met all NATO membership criteria and warned that excluding it from the Alliance's first expansion could provoke problems throughout Eastern Europe.

In an address to Britain's Royal United Services Institute for Defence Studies, the king said Romanians fully backed their country's longshot bid to be part of the first wave of enlargement to be announced in July.
Exclusion, he said, would be viewed as a rebuff to the country's drive to build a prosperous post-communist society.

"If, having exerted all efforts to meet the criteria, new reasons are found to exclude Romania, the West will have little credibility not only in my country but... in the entire region," the king said. A text of his speech was released in advance.

"Those who say back home that we must pay no attention to what the West expects from us will appear to be vindicated and all the gloom and doom scenarios feared by the West could become self-fulfilling prophecies."
Michael, 75, was forced by pro-Moscow communists to abdicate and leave Romania in 1947 and has since lived in Switzerland.
Michael visited his homeland for only the second time last month after a new centrist government restored his citizenship.

President Emil Constantinescu, who ousted an ex-communist in last year's elections, commissioned him to plead in favour of Romania's bid to be admitted to NATO at the same time as favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
After his stay in Britain, where he has blood ties to the royal family, the king was due to visit the Netherlands as part of a tour of NATO constitutional monarchies.
A European Commission study released this week showed Romanians to be the keenest people in eastern Europe for NATO membership, with 80 percent of those polled in favour.
France has led a number of NATO members enthusiastically backing early admission for Romania and Slovenia.
But after last week's U.S.-Russian summit, at which Moscow agreed to minimise its objections to enlargement, Romanian officials acknowledged that their bid remained a long shot.
In his address, Michael said the government's commitment to reform and the signature of a treaty burying longstanding differences with Hungary made Romania a worthy candidate.

Admitting Hungary but leaving Romania out, he said, could sour ties between the neighbours and jeopardise Bucharest's efforts to conclude a similar treaty with Ukraine. It could send the wrong signal to Turkey, discontent at delays in its bid for European Union membership.
"Almost regardless of how moderate and understanding the government in Bucharest is, certain consequences follow from any exclusion and they are outside the control of most politicians," he said.
